blocks.text: The chapter uses a regular genealogy pattern: the age at which a son is fathered, further years and other children, a total lifespan, and a closing notice. This pattern carries the line from Adam through Seth toward Noah. Its repeated statement, “and he died,” makes mortality a persistent refrain, while Enoch’s account interrupts that refrain. The opening also links humanity’s creation in God’s likeness with Seth being born in Adam’s likeness and image.

The ages and lifespans in Genesis 5 are not identical in the Masoretic Text, the Septuagint, and the Samaritan Pentateuch—three textual traditions of Genesis. The differences raise a textual question about the chapter’s numbers without, on their own, settling which reading is original or allowing a single chronology to be calculated. Within the genealogy, Enoch receives an unusual notice: he walks with God and is taken by God instead of receiving the ordinary death formula. The line then reaches Noah, whose name Lamech connects with hoped-for relief from toil and from the cursed ground.

Read as a literary unit, the genealogy provides continuity from Adam to Noah while holding together repeated mortality and Lamech’s hope connected with Noah. This helps explain why the chapter is more than a modern chronology table: its orderly succession advances the narrative while drawing attention to the recurring deaths, Enoch’s exception, and the expectation expressed at Noah’s birth.

sections.title: More than a list of dates

blocks.text: Genesis moves from universal origins in chapters 1–11 to the ancestral family narratives in chapters 12–50, ending with Jacob’s household in Egypt. Genesis 5 belongs to the opening movement, where genealogy is one of the forms that carries the story forward.

Genesis 1–11 belongs to an ancient Near Eastern literary environment in which creation, flood, genealogy, and city-building traditions were also discussed. Comparisons may clarify shared motifs and cultural questions, but they do not by themselves establish direct copying or determine how Genesis should be interpreted.
